claims.claim: The duration of continuous call elements (syllables) in male mouse vocalisations follows a bimodal distribution with a majority of short syllables (local maximum = 23 ms, 86% with durations shorter than 63 ms) and a minority of long syllables (local maximum = 88 ms, 14% with durations longer than 63 ms).
claims.source: Across the set of recorded male vocalisations, the duration of continuous call elements, or syllables, followed a bimodal distribution, with a majority of short syllables (local maximum = 23 ms, 86% [2039/2373] of recorded syllables with durations shorter than 63 ms [local minimum]) and a minority of long syllables (local maximum = 88 ms, 14% [334/2373] of recorded syllables with durations longer than 63 ms, Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the authors' recordings shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Male mouse calls are restricted to the ultrasonic frequency range, with maximal energy occurring around 76 kHz and spanning a bandwidth of 16 kHz (68–84 kHz).
claims.source: These male calls were restricted to the ultrasonic frequency range, with the maximal energy in individual syllables occurring around 76 kHz (median peak frequency and 95% confidence interval [CI], 76 ± 0.3 kHz, n = 2373 syllables) and spanning a bandwidth of 16 kHz ([68–84 kHz]; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the authors' data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Individual syllables in male mouse songs are organised in temporally regular sequences with inter-syllable intervals concentrated around 104 ± 2 ms.
claims.source: Individual syllables were organised in temporally regular sequences and often started at an approximately constant time delay from each other (Holy and Guo, 2005; Castellucci et al., 2018), as evidenced by the narrow concentration of inter-syllable interval durations around 104 ± 2 ms (median inter-syllable interval and 95% CI; interquartile range of syllable interval = 61 ms, n = 2322 syllables followed by another syllable within 2 s; Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' quantitative data (Figure 1D) and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Male courtship songs are attractive to sexually receptive female mice.
claims.source: These courtship songs are attractive to sexually receptive females (Pomerantz et al., 1983), who respond to song playback with approach behaviour (Asaba et al., 2014b; Shepard and Liu, 2011; Chabout et al., 2015; Musolf et al., 2015; Hammerschmidt et al., 2009; Asaba et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies demonstrating female attraction to male songs.

claims.claim: Male songs facilitate copulatory success.
claims.source: Male songs facilitate copulatory success (Nomoto et al., 2018) and are thought to serve as fitness displays (Egnor and Seagraves, 2016; Hoffmann et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Mouse listeners are able to detect and report spectro-temporal differences between individual ultrasonic call elements.
claims.source: On the one hand, reinforcement learning experiments have shown that mouse listeners are able to detect and report spectro-temporal differences between individual ultrasonic call elements (Neilans et al., 2014; Holfoth et al., 2014), indicating that mice are perceptually sensitive to a wide range of acoustic features in the vocalisations.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous reinforcement learning studies.

claims.claim: Female mice use certain acoustic characteristics in male songs to discriminate between social contexts, singer species, strain, and kin.
claims.source: On the other hand, experiments using ethologically relevant place preference paradigms without external reward have shown that females use, or are behaviourally sensitive to, certain acoustic characteristics in male songs to guide social decisions, such as discriminating between social contexts (Chabout et al., 2015), singer species (Musolf et al., 2015), strain (Asaba et al., 2014a; Sugimoto et al., 2011), and kin (Musolf et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous behavioral studies.

claims.claim: Female mice significantly discriminate between song playback and silence in a place preference assay (n = 29 sessions, mean preference index significantly different from 0, one-sample t-test, t(28) = 2.81, p=0.0088).
claims.source: The behaviour of female listeners tested in this paradigm significantly discriminated between song playback and silence (n = 29 sessions, mean preference index significantly different from 0, one-sample t-test, t(28) = 2.81, p=0.0088; Figure 2H), and mouse listeners were overwhelmingly attracted to the playback of our subset of male songs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the authors' behavioral data shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: Mouse listeners demonstrate significant approach response after as little as 16.9 s of song playback across four sound presentation trials.
claims.source: Mouse listeners demonstrated significant approach response after as little as 16.9 s of sound playback across the four sound presentation trials (normalised cumulative time in speaker zone significantly different from 0, one-sample t-test, p<0.05; Figure 2K), with preference further increasing over the course of song playback.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of temporal data shown in Figure 2K.

claims.claim: The sequential organisation of syllables in male songs is not necessary for normal female approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs randomised songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = 0.126, p=0.90).
claims.source: We found that the sequential organisation of syllables in the male songs was not necessary for normal approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs randomised songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = 0.126, p=0.90; Figure 3A, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and randomized songs.

claims.claim: Temporal reversal of vocal sequences does not significantly affect female approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs reversed songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = –1.46, p=0.16).
claims.source: Temporal reversal of the vocal sequence did not significantly affect females' approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs reversed songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = –1.46, p=0.16; Figure 3C, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and reversed songs.

claims.claim: Female listeners are not relying on global cues reflecting the overall structure of male song sequences when selecting which sound source to approach.
claims.source: Together, these observations suggest that female listeners are not relying on global cues reflecting the overall structure of male song sequences when selecting which sound source to approach.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the results of multiple manipulations (randomization and reversal) showing no behavioral effect.

claims.claim: Females approach intact and phase-scrambled song playback similarly (mean preference index in response to intact vs phase-scrambled songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(22) = –0.27, p=0.79).
claims.source: Females approached the intact and phase-scrambled song playback similarly (mean preference index in response to intact vs phase-scrambled songs did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(22) = –0.27, p=0.79; Figure 3E, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and phase-scrambled songs.

claims.claim: Comparing intact songs with sequences of pure tones at the peak syllable frequency (76 kHz) fails to elicit differential approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs pure tone sequences did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = 0.034, p=0.97).
claims.source: Second, comparing intact songs with more drastically simplified sound sequences that stripped down each syllable into a pure tone at the peak syllable frequency (76 kHz) also failed to elicit differential approach behaviour (mean preference index in response to intact vs pure tone sequences did not differ from zero, one-sample t-test, t(20) = 0.034, p=0.97; Figure 3G and Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact songs and pure tone sequences.

claims.claim: Female behaviour is robust to the removal of fast spectro-temporal structure in syllables when sound energy is still present at the natural syllable peak frequency.
claims.source: Together, these findings show that female behaviour was robust to the removal of fast spectro-temporal structure in the syllables, at least when sound energy was still present at the natural syllable peak frequency.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the results of phase-scrambling and pure tone manipulations showing no behavioral effect.

claims.claim: Females are highly sensitive to the disruption of song temporal regularity and preferentially approach intact over irregular song playback (mean preference index in response to intact vs irregular songs significantly differed from zero, one-sample t-test, t(23) = 3.43, p=0.00023).
claims.source: Interestingly, females were highly sensitive to the disruption of song temporal regularity and preferentially approached intact over irregular song playback (mean preference index in response to intact vs irregular songs significantly differed from zero, one-sample t-test, t(23) = 3.43, p=0.00023, Figure 4E, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and temporally irregular songs.

claims.claim: Mouse listeners start to show sustained preference for regular over irregular songs after 85.4 s of sound playback.
claims.source: On average, mouse listeners started to show this sustained preference for regular over irregular songs after 85.4 s of sound playback (normalised cumulative time in speaker zone significantly different from 0, one-sample t-test, p<0.05; Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by temporal analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Female listeners do not show consistent behavioural preference when playback of intact songs is contrasted with super-regular songs (one-sample t-test, t(21) = 1.48, p=0.15).
claims.source: Female listeners did not show any consistent behavioural preference when the playback of intact songs was contrasted with that of super-regular songs (one-sample t-test, t(21) = 1.48, p=0.15; Figure 4H, right).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing intact and super-regular songs.

claims.claim: The rhythmicity of natural male songs is already sufficiently salient to reach the criterion for approach behaviour by female listeners and cannot be improved by additional regularisation of syllable onsets.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that the rhythmicity of natural male songs is already sufficiently salient to reach the criterion for approach behaviour by female listeners and cannot be improved by additional regularisation of syllable onsets.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of preference for super-regular over intact songs.

claims.claim: Female mice monitor temporal regularity in male songs during courtship behaviour.
claims.source: The results show that female mice monitor temporal regularity in male songs, while their behaviour was unaffected by changes in the song sequential organisation or the fine acoustic structure of individual syllables.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from multiple behavioral experiments.

claims.claim: Temporal regularity may represent an acoustic signature of singer fitness.
claims.source: The findings highlight the selective extraction of song temporal regularity, which may be an acoustic signature of singer fitness, as an effective, potentially evolutionarily conserved behavioural strategy for the sensory compression of complex vocal sequences during goal-directed social behaviour.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claims.claim: Neurons across the mouse auditory system are tuned to different spectro-temporal features in song syllables.
claims.source: On the one hand, neurons across the mouse auditory system are tuned to different spectro-temporal features in song syllables, and mouse listeners have been shown to be perceptually sensitive to, or able to detect, the acoustic manipulations of individual syllables used in the current study.
claims.evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about auditory system tuning properties.

claims.claim: Externally rewarded reinforcement learning and associated sharpening of sensory acuity and neuronal tuning likely bias and amplify the perceptual ability of a naive animal.
claims.source: However, such externally rewarded reinforcement learning and the associated sharpening of sensory acuity and neuronal tuning likely bias and amplify the perceptual ability of a naive animal (Fritz et al., 2005; Fritz et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on perceptual learning.

claims.claim: In naturalistic settings, social behaviour requires the selective monitoring of specific informative sensory features while cognitively suppressing or ignoring other dimensions that may be perceptible.
claims.source: On the other hand, social behaviour in naturalistic settings requires the selective monitoring of specific informative sensory features, while cognitively suppressing or ignoring other dimensions that may however be perceptible, as classically demonstrated in the toad's visual system during prey capture (Wachowitz and Ewert, 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim draws on established principles from sensory neuroscience, supported by a citation to work in toads.

claims.claim: In the context of ethologically valid behaviour, female listeners show behavioural invariance to several acoustic features that they are, or can be trained to become, perceptually sensitive to.
claims.source: Our work complements previous studies that quantified the upper bounds of mouse hearing sensitivity. We show that, in the context of an ethologically valid behaviour, female listeners show behavioural invariance to several acoustic features that they are, or can be trained to become, perceptually sensitive to.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the main conclusion from the behavioral experiments.

claims.claim: Songs from male mice demonstrate characteristic sequential features, with short syllables typically dominating the beginning of a vocal phrase.
claims.source: Indeed, songs from male mice have been shown to demonstrate some characteristic sequential features, with short syllables typically dominating the beginning of a vocal phrase (Chabout et al., 2015; Matsumoto and Okanoya, 2016; Castellucci et al., 2018; Castellucci et al., 2016; Hertz et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies characterizing song structure.

claims.claim: During courtship behaviour, females monitor the presence/absence or relative occurrence of specific syllable types independent of the syllable order.
claims.source: While mouse listeners are known to perceptually discriminate between syllable types differing in their spectro-temporal features (Neilans et al., 2014), our finding that female approach behaviour was not affected by a shuffling of the syllable sequence indicates that, during courtship behaviour, females monitor the presence/absence or relative occurrence of specific syllable types, or other acoustic features of the songs, independent of the syllable order.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral invariance to syllable order randomization.

claims.claim: Chabout et al., 2015 showed that female listeners discriminated between syntactically simple and complex songs produced by males in different social contexts.
claims.source: Our result also disambiguates previous findings on mouse sensitivity to syntactic information in male songs: Chabout et al., 2015 previously showed, in a similar behavioural paradigm, that female listeners discriminated between syntactically simple and complex songs produced by males in different social contexts.
claims.evidence: The claim describes findings from a previous study.

claims.claim: Listeners may have been primarily exploiting differences in repertoire composition rather than syllable sequencing to discriminate songs produced from different social contexts.
claims.source: Songs produced in the two tested social contexts differed both in the first-order syllable sequencing and in the composition of the syllable repertoire. Our finding on females' behavioural insensitivity to syllable order thus suggests that listeners may have been primarily exploiting differences in repertoire composition to discriminate and ultimately select songs produced from a specific social context.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the current study's findings about syllable order insensitivity, reinterpreting previous results.

claims.claim: Female listeners do not strongly rely on the global structure of the syllable sequence during courtship behaviour.
claims.source: Thus, our results show that female listeners do not strongly rely on the global structure of the syllable sequence during courtship behaviour.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the findings from manipulations of global song structure.

claims.claim: Sound energy in and around a critical band corresponding to the syllable frequency range, displayed at the natural temporal organisation of male songs, is a sufficient approximation of male courtship songs to drive female approach behaviour.
claims.source: Thus, the evidence suggests that sound energy in and around a critical band corresponding to the syllable frequency range, displayed at the natural temporal organisation of male songs, is a sufficient approximation of male courtship songs to drive female approach behaviour.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral results with pure tone sequences and the discussion of previous studies.

claims.claim: As long as the temporal structure of pup calls is maintained, pup retrieval behaviour is robust to the removal of most of the spectral structure of ultrasonic pup isolation calls.
claims.source: Our and others' results on female courtship behaviour complement the body of work on maternal behaviour by lactating mothers: as long as the temporal structure of pup calls is maintained, pup retrieval behaviour is robust to the removal of most of the spectral structure of ultrasonic pup isolation calls (Ehret and Haack, 1982), and three-harmonic stack approximations of sonic wriggling calls elicit normal maternal responses (Gaub and Ehret, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on maternal behavior.

claims.claim: The intelligibility of speech degraded in the spectral domain remains partially preserved if it is shaped with the correct amplitude envelopes.
claims.source: Similar importance of temporal patterns for the perception of social communication, over the fine acoustic structure of individual elements, has been demonstrated behaviourally in other animal species, including humans: as illustrated in vocoded speech, the intelligibility of speech degraded in the spectral domain remains partially preserved if it is shaped with the correct amplitude envelopes (Shannon et al., 1995; Van Tasell et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on human speech perception.

claims.claim: Temporal regularity in the song is the only feature observed to be extracted by female listeners from male acoustic courtship displays among the subset of acoustic features tested in this study.
claims.source: Of the subset of acoustic features tested in this study, temporal regularity in the song was the only feature we observed to be extracted by female listeners from male acoustic courtship displays.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding from the series of behavioral experiments.

claims.claim: Temporal regularity is attractive to females in the context of vocal-based mate selection.
claims.source: We found that mouse listeners preferentially approached intact over irregular courtship songs, suggesting that regularity is attractive to females in the context of vocal-based mate selection.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral preference for regular over irregular songs.

claims.claim: The temporal regularity observed in mouse songs is a consequence of breathing patterns regulating the production of syllables by the emitter as individual calls are generated following the onset of exhalation.
claims.source: The temporal regularity observed in mouse songs is a consequence of breathing patterns regulating the production of syllables by the emitter as individual calls are generated following the onset of exhalation (Tschida et al., 2019; Castellucci et al., 2018; Sirotin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on vocal production mechanisms.

claims.claim: Disruption to the temporal regularity of male song may result from irregular breathing cycles and thus 'stuttering' singing by the male, or by the inability to sustain bouts of vocal production of sufficient duration.
claims.source: Disruption to the temporal regularity of male song, as artificially introduced in this study, may, for instance, result from irregular breathing cycles and thus 'stuttering' singing by the male, or by the inability to sustain bouts of vocal production of sufficient duration to elicit a salient percept of regularity in the listener.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential biological mechanisms underlying temporal irregularity.

claims.claim: Songs by Foxp2 knockout mice contain rhythmic irregularities.
claims.source: A recent study of courtship songs by Foxp2 knockout mice provided direct evidence for a link between male emitter fitness and song temporal regularity by showing songs by mutant mice contain rhythmic irregularities (Castellucci et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on Foxp2 knockout mice.

claims.claim: Temporal predictability facilitates auditory detection of near-threshold stimuli compared to an identical aperiodic sequence.
claims.source: From the perspective of the listener, temporal predictability has been shown to facilitate auditory detection of near-threshold stimuli compared to an identical aperiodic sequence (Lawrance et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on temporal predictability.

claims.claim: In human listeners, speech intelligibility is disrupted by temporal jittering of sentences.
claims.source: Additionally, in human listeners, speech intelligibility is disrupted by temporal jittering the sentences (Ghitza and Greenberg, 2009; Pichora-Fuller et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on human speech perception.

claims.claim: Temporal regularity may represent an acoustic cue signalling the fitness or suitability of the potential mating partner to the listener.
claims.source: Thus, perhaps by improving the perceptual signal-to-noise ratio of male courtship songs, temporal regularity may represent an acoustic cue signalling the fitness or suitability of the potential mating partner to the listener (Egnor and Seagraves, 2016), to which we show that socially motivated listeners are highly attuned to.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional interpretation supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Natural mouse songs might already be at ceiling in terms of the perceptual saliency of their temporal regularity and their attractiveness to female listeners.
claims.source: Female behaviour did not appear to discriminate between intact songs and an artificial 'super-regular' version of the songs, suggesting that natural mouse songs might already be at ceiling in terms of the perceptual saliency of their temporal regularity, and therefore, their attractiveness to female listeners.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of preference for super-regular songs.

claims.claim: Neuronal responses in barrel cortex respond indistinguishably to lightly temporally jittered and perfectly regular sequences of whisker deflections when the stimulus presentation rate is slower than 20 Hz.
claims.source: In the somatosensory system, neuronal responses in barrel cortex responded indistinguishably to lightly temporally jittered and perfectly regular sequences of whisker deflections, when the stimulus presentation rate was slower than 20 Hz (Lak et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on somatosensory processing.

claims.claim: At natural syllable rates of mouse songs, removing low temporal jitter present in intact songs to create super-regular songs may not significantly impact perceptually relevant neuronal substrates.
claims.source: In a hypothesis that remains to be directly tested in the auditory system, it is thus possible that, at the natural syllable rates of mouse songs, removing the low temporal jitter present in intact songs to create super-regular songs does not significantly impact on perceptually relevant neuronal substrates.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis based on findings from the somatosensory system.

claims.claim: The syllable rate in mouse songs (~7 Hz) broadly matches with that of other mammalian vocal patterns such as monkey vocalisations and human speech.
claims.source: The syllable rate in mouse songs (~7 Hz; Holy and Guo, 2005) broadly matches with that of other mammalian vocal patterns such as monkey vocalisations and human speech (Ghazanfar and Takahashi, 2014; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on vocal patterns across species.

claims.claim: The stimulus presentation rate in mouse songs is directly determined by the breathing rhythm of the singer.
claims.source: On the one hand, this stimulus presentation rate in mouse songs is directly determined by the breathing rhythm of the singer.
claims.evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about vocal production mechanisms.

claims.claim: Active sensation during whisking and sniffing operates within the frequency range of both respiratory-coupled oscillations and the hippocampal theta rhythm in rodents.
claims.source: Given that active sensation during whisking and sniffing operates within the frequency range of both respiratory-coupled oscillations (Tort et al., 2018) and the hippocampal theta rhythm in rodents (Kleinfeld et al., 2006; Kepecs et al., 2007; Grion et al., 2016; Kleinfeld et al., 2016), similar constraints may be placed on the cortical mechanisms of hearing (Schroeder et al., 2010), especially during natural behaviour.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on sensory processing and oscillations.

claims.claim: The syllable rate in mouse songs generally corresponds to the timescale of slow amplitude envelope in human speech, which contributes to the identification of both prosodic and syllabic content.
claims.source: On the other hand, the syllable rate in mouse songs generally corresponds to the timescale of slow amplitude envelope in human speech, which is known to contribute to the identification of both prosodic and syllabic content (Peelle and Davis, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on speech processing.

claims.claim: Vocal sequences such as human speech and mouse songs contain sufficiently salient temporal regularity to allow listeners to make predictions about the incoming signal.
claims.source: While vocal sequences such as human speech and mouse songs are quasi-periodic rather than metronomically regular signals, they both contain sufficiently salient temporal regularity to allow listeners to make predictions about the incoming signal (Peelle and Davis, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on speech processing.

claims.claim: Cortical theta oscillations in the 4–8 Hz range entrain to the slow temporal envelope modulations in speech and may play a role in parsing continuous sensory input by coordinating neuronal excitability to optimally support the decoding of phonemes.
claims.source: An influential model of speech processing proposes that cortical theta oscillations in the 4–8 Hz range entrain to the slow temporal envelope modulations in speech and may play a role in parsing continuous sensory input by coordinating neuronal excitability to optimally support the decoding of phonemes (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous theoretical model of speech processing.

claims.claim: The results identify a key role of temporal regularity, but invariance to global and local song structure, in the goal-directed use of vocal patterns by female listeners.
claims.source: In summary, we used an ethologically driven approach to evaluate the behavioural relevance of several acoustic features in mouse communication. Our results identify a key role of temporal regularity, but invariance to global and local song structure, in the goal-directed use of vocal patterns by female listeners.
claims.evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: The selective monitoring of temporal regularity in communication sounds is an effective, potentially evolutionarily conserved behavioural strategy for the sensory compression of complex vocal sequences during mammalian vocal perception.
claims.source: The findings highlight the selective monitoring of temporal regularity in communication sounds as an effective, potentially evolutionarily conserved behavioural strategy for the sensory compression of complex vocal sequences during mammalian vocal perception.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the findings, proposing evolutionary significance.

claims.claim: A total of 83 female C57Bl/6J inbred mice participated in the experiments.
claims.source: A total of 83 female C57Bl/6J inbred mice (Mus musculus, Charles River Laboratories, UK) participated in the experiments.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claims.claim: Mice participated in the playback experiments between the ages of 5–11 wk (mean = 9 wk).
claims.source: Mice participated in the playback experiments between the ages of 5–11 wk (mean = 9 wk; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the age range of experimental subjects.

claims.claim: The stimulus set used in playback experiments consisted of seven distinct songs produced by C57BL/6 male mice aged 22 wk on average (median age, range [10–27 wk]).
claims.source: This stimulus set was composed of seven distinct songs produced by C57BL/6 male mice aged 22 wk on average (median age, range [10–27 wk]) in response to the presentation of female urine.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the characteristics of the acoustic stimuli used.

claims.claim: The songs varied in duration, lasting on average 33.4 s (median duration, range [13–41 s]), and were composed of an average of 145 syllables (median, range [95–186]).
claims.source: The songs varied in duration, lasting on average 33.4 s (median duration, range [13–41 s]), and were composed of an average of 145 syllables (median, range [95–186]).
claims.evidence: The claim describes quantitative characteristics of the song stimuli.

claims.claim: Olfactory stimulation from mixed male bedding samples was present throughout the testing session to increase sexual arousal and motivation in female listeners.
claims.source: Importantly, olfactory stimulation from mixed male bedding samples placed under each of the loudspeakers was present throughout the testing session in order to increase sexual arousal and motivation in the female listeners (Hammerschmidt et al., 2009; Asaba et al., 2014a) and create a multisensory coherent approximation of a natural social situation.
claims.evidence: The claim describes an experimental design feature supported by citations.

claims.claim: Young female C57Bl/6 mice participated once in the playback experiment while in the fertile (proestrus or oestrus) stage of their oestrous cycle.
claims.source: Young female C57Bl/6 mice (aged 5–11 wk; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) participated once in the playback experiment, while in the fertile (proestrus or oestrus) stage of their oestrous cycle (as assessed by vaginal cytology, see 'Methods').
claims.evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol for subject selection.

claims.claim: The preference for song over silence was robust to different lengths of the speaker zone used to calculate the preference index.
claims.source: The preference for song over silence was robust to different lengths of the speaker zone used to calculate the preference index (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim describes a control analysis showing robustness of the main finding.

claims.claim: The build-up of preferential approach to song was evident in the vast majority of animals and mostly sustained over a behavioural session.
claims.source: The build-up of preferential approach to song was evident in the vast majority of animals, mostly sustained over a behavioural session (Figure 2L), and similar across the four sound presentation trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the temporal dynamics of the behavioral response shown in figures.

claims.claim: The lack of sensitivity to syllable sequence structure was not caused by the selection of specific temporal or spatial parameters for analysis.
claims.source: This confirms that the lack of sensitivity to syllable sequence structure we observe here was not caused by the selection of specific temporal or spatial parameters for analysis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from control analyses showing robustness across different parameters.

claims.claim: This behavioural invariance to changes in the syllable order was apparent at all timepoints of song set playback as well as at different speaker zone lengths.
claims.source: This behavioural invariance to changes in the syllable order was apparent at all timepoints of song set playback (Figure 3B), as well as at different speaker zone lengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), and was comparable across the four sound presentation trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim describes control analyses showing robustness of the finding.

claims.claim: This lack of behavioural sensitivity to song temporal reversal was present throughout sound playback in the vast majority of animals tested.
claims.source: This lack of behavioural sensitivity to song temporal reversal was present throughout sound playback in the vast majority of animals tested (Figure 3D), across the sound presentation trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and for different spatial regions of interest (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the consistency of the behavioral finding across different analyses.

claims.claim: These two instances of behavioural insensitivity to changes in the syllable acoustic trajectories were robust to variations in temporal and spatial parameters used for analysis.
claims.source: These two instances of behavioural insensitivity to changes in the syllable acoustic trajectories were robust to variations in temporal (Figure 3F and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G) and spatial (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and G) parameters used for analysis.
claims.evidence: The claim describes control analyses showing robustness of findings.

claims.claim: The interquartile range of syllable interval in irregular songs is 134 ms compared to 61 ms for intact songs.
claims.source: To do this, we generated a set of temporally irregular songs that consisted of the same syllable sequence with a broadened distribution of silent pauses compared to intact songs (interquartile range of syllable interval in irregular songs = 134 ms compared to 61 ms for intact songs; Figure 4A, B and E, left, and Supplementary file 6).
claims.evidence: The claim describes quantitative characteristics of the manipulated stimuli.

claims.claim: The sensitivity to temporal regularity was robust and similarly strong across all sizes of speaker zones.
claims.source: The sensitivity to temporal regularity was robust and similarly strong across all sizes of speaker zones (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim describes a control analysis showing robustness of the finding.

claims.claim: The temporal profile of approach behaviour of a majority of animals favoured intact, regular songs over the course of a session and across sound presentation trials.
claims.source: The temporal profile of approach behaviour of a majority of animals favoured intact, regular songs over the course of a session (Figure 4G), and across sound presentation trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the consistency of the behavioral response shown in figures.

claims.claim: The longer latency to behavioural discrimination after song onset when discriminating between two concurrent sound streams compared to approaching intact song playback over silence might reflect the need for additional accumulation of evidence and temporal integration.
claims.source: This longer latency to behavioural discrimination after song onset compared to when approaching intact song playback over silence (16.9 s, Figure 2K) might reflect the need for additional accumulation of evidence and temporal integration when discriminating between the two concurrent sound streams.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the difference in response latencies.

claims.claim: The interquartile range of syllable interval in super-regular songs is 24 ms compared to 61 ms for intact songs.
claims.source: To this end, we created a set of highly rhythmic songs in which the silent breaks were modified such that the onset of the syllables in each song occurred exactly at the dominant inter-syllable interval, effectively narrowing the distribution of inter-syllable times (interquartile range of syllable interval in super-regular songs = 24 ms compared to 61 ms for intact songs; Figure 4C, D and H, left, and Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: The claim describes quantitative characteristics of the manipulated stimuli.

claims.claim: This behavioural invariance to improvements of the songs' temporal regularity remained when tested at different timepoints during song playback or using different spatial parameters for analysis.
claims.source: This behavioural invariance to improvements of the songs' temporal regularity remained when tested at different timepoints during song playback (Figure 4I) or using different spatial parameters for analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim describes control analyses showing robustness of the finding.

claims.claim: Sessions in which the animal displayed a clear side bias were excluded from the analysis (29% ± 7% of behavioural sessions excluded due to side bias, mean and 95% CI).
claims.source: Sessions in which the animal displayed a clear side bias (consistent preference for the left or right side of the behavioural box despite changes in the sound playback side, evaluated as all four trials showing a positive, or all negative, difference between the times in the left and right speaker zones) were excluded from the analysis (29% ± 7% of behavioural sessions excluded due to side bias, mean and 95% CI).
claims.evidence: The claim describes the data exclusion criteria and the proportion of excluded sessions.

results.result: Male C57Bl/6 mice produce ultrasonic courtship songs consisting of frequency-modulated syllables with characteristic acoustic properties: bimodal duration distribution (peaks at 23 ms and 88 ms), peak frequency around 76 kHz, and temporally regular organization with inter-syllable intervals around 104 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging quantitative characterization of male mouse vocalizations supported by direct measurements (Figure 1) and citations to prior work. The acoustic parameters are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes (n=2373 syllables) and statistical measures (medians, confidence intervals). Claims C57-C58 provide methodological details about the stimulus set used in experiments.

results.result: Female mice significantly prefer male song playback over silence in a place preference assay, with significant discrimination emerging after 16.9 s of playback and sustained preference across behavioral sessions.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 demonstrates significant preference with appropriate statistics (t(28)=2.81, p=0.0088, n=29 sessions). Claims C11, C61-C62 provide temporal dynamics and robustness analyses showing the effect is consistent across different spatial parameters and time points. The experimental design includes appropriate controls (silent baseline, alternating playback sides).

results.result: Female approach behavior is invariant to manipulations of global song structure, including syllable order randomization (p=0.90) and temporal reversal (p=0.16), indicating females do not rely on sequential organization or global temporal structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 provide direct statistical evidence of behavioral invariance with non-significant results and appropriate sample sizes (n=21 sessions each). Claims C63-C65 demonstrate robustness across different analysis parameters. The null results are appropriately interpreted as evidence for behavioral invariance rather than lack of statistical power, given the significant effects observed in other conditions.

results.result: Female approach behavior is robust to removal of spectro-temporal structure in syllables, showing no preference between intact songs and either phase-scrambled syllables (p=0.79) or pure tone sequences (p=0.97), suggesting sound energy at the peak frequency with natural temporal organization is sufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 provide statistical evidence of behavioral invariance to syllable acoustic manipulations with appropriate sample sizes (n=22-23 sessions). Claim C66 demonstrates robustness across analysis parameters. Claim C33 provides a reasonable inference about sufficient acoustic features, though this interpretation could benefit from additional testing with frequency-shifted stimuli.

results.result: Female mice are highly sensitive to disruptions of temporal regularity, preferentially approaching intact over temporally irregular songs (t(23)=3.43, p=0.00023), with sustained preference emerging after 85.4 s of playback.
results.evaluation: Claim C18 provides strong statistical evidence with appropriate sample size (n=24 sessions) and highly significant p-value. Claims C67-C69 provide quantitative characterization of the manipulation (IQR increased from 61 to 134 ms) and demonstrate robustness and consistency of the effect. This represents the only acoustic feature tested that elicited significant behavioral discrimination.

results.result: Female mice show no preference between intact and super-regular songs (p=0.15), suggesting natural song temporal regularity is already at ceiling for perceptual saliency and attractiveness.
results.evaluation: Claim C20 provides statistical evidence of no preference with appropriate sample size (n=22 sessions). Claim C71 documents the manipulation (IQR reduced from 61 to 24 ms). Claims C21 and C44 provide reasonable interpretations of the null result as a ceiling effect, though alternative explanations (e.g., perceptual equivalence of natural and super-regular timing) are not fully excluded.

results.result: Female mice selectively monitor temporal regularity in male songs during courtship behavior while showing behavioral invariance to sequential organization and syllable spectro-temporal structure.
results.evaluation: These summary claims (C22, C27, C36, C53) accurately synthesize the main experimental findings from the behavioral manipulations. The conclusion is well-supported by the pattern of results: significant discrimination only for temporal regularity manipulations, with invariance to all other tested features. The claims appropriately distinguish between perceptual sensitivity (what mice can detect) and behavioral relevance (what they use).

results.result: During courtship, females monitor the presence/absence or relative occurrence of specific syllable types independent of syllable order, potentially reinterpreting previous findings that females may exploit repertoire composition rather than syllable sequencing to discriminate songs from different social contexts.
results.evaluation: Claim C29 provides a reasonable inference from the syllable randomization results (C12). Claim C31 offers a plausible reinterpretation of Chabout et al. 2015 findings based on the current results. However, this reinterpretation is speculative and would require direct testing with stimuli that independently manipulate repertoire composition and syllable order.

results.result: Temporal regularity may represent an acoustic signature of singer fitness and an evolutionarily conserved strategy for sensory compression of complex vocal sequences during mammalian vocal perception.
results.evaluation: These claims (C23, C37, C43, C54) are explicitly speculative interpretations of the behavioral findings. While the behavioral data on temporal regularity sensitivity are solid, the functional interpretations regarding fitness signaling and evolutionary conservation require additional evidence (e.g., correlation between male temporal regularity and fitness measures, cross-species comparisons, fitness consequences of female choices).

results.result: Temporal regularity in mouse songs is determined by breathing patterns during vocal production, and disruptions may result from irregular breathing or inability to sustain vocal bouts, with evidence from Foxp2 knockout mice showing rhythmic irregularities.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is well-supported by citations to previous studies on vocal production mechanisms. Claim C40 provides supporting evidence from genetic manipulations. Claim C39 is speculative but reasonable given the established link between breathing and vocal production. These claims appropriately contextualize the behavioral findings within production mechanisms.

results.result: Male courtship songs are attractive to females, facilitate copulatory success, and females can use acoustic characteristics to make social discriminations, as established by previous research.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 accurately summarize prior work with appropriate citations. These provide essential context for the current study but represent established knowledge rather than new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims accurately represent the cited work.

results.result: While mice can be trained to detect spectro-temporal features in syllables, ethologically valid behavior requires selective monitoring of informative features while suppressing perceptible but irrelevant dimensions.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 appropriately cite prior work on auditory tuning and perceptual learning. Claim C27 provides a reasonable synthesis distinguishing perceptual capacity from behavioral relevance. The argument that reinforcement learning may amplify perceptual abilities beyond natural behavior is well-supported by citations and provides important context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Male mouse songs demonstrate characteristic sequential features with short syllables dominating phrase beginnings, and previous work showed females discriminate between syntactically simple and complex songs from different social contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C28 and C30 accurately describe prior findings with appropriate citations. These provide context for the current study's investigation of sequential structure. The claims appear to accurately represent the cited work.

results.result: Similar importance of temporal patterns over spectral structure has been demonstrated in other contexts including maternal behavior in mice and speech perception in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 appropriately cite prior work showing temporal pattern importance in other behavioral contexts. These provide valuable comparative context suggesting the current findings may reflect a general principle. The citations appear appropriate and accurately represented.

results.result: Temporal predictability facilitates auditory detection and speech intelligibility is disrupted by temporal jittering, as shown in previous studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 cite prior work on the perceptual benefits of temporal regularity. These provide mechanistic context for why temporal regularity might be behaviorally relevant. The citations appear appropriate.

results.result: Neuronal responses in barrel cortex show indistinguishable responses to lightly jittered versus regular whisker deflections below 20 Hz, suggesting that removing low temporal jitter at natural syllable rates may not impact perceptually relevant neural substrates.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 appropriately cites prior work in somatosensory cortex. However, claim C46 is explicitly speculative and extrapolates across sensory modalities without direct evidence. The hypothesis is reasonable but requires direct testing in the auditory system. This speculation is appropriately qualified by the authors.

results.result: The syllable rate in mouse songs (~7 Hz) matches other mammalian vocalizations, is determined by breathing rhythm, corresponds to speech envelope timescales, and may relate to theta oscillations that could support temporal parsing of vocal sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C50-C52 appropriately cite prior work on vocal timing across species and neural oscillations. Claim C48 states established knowledge about breathing and vocalization. Claim C49 is more speculative, proposing potential constraints on auditory processing based on other sensory modalities. These claims provide valuable theoretical context, though the proposed links to auditory processing mechanisms remain hypothetical.

results.result: The study used 83 female C57Bl/6J mice aged 5-11 weeks tested during fertile cycle stages, with playback of seven male songs and olfactory stimulation present, excluding 29% of sessions due to side bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60, C73 provide methodological details that are clearly documented. The sample sizes are adequate, age ranges are specified, and the exclusion criteria for side bias (29±7%) are transparently reported. The inclusion of olfactory stimulation (C59) is appropriately justified by citations. These methodological details support reproducibility.

results.result: The longer latency to discrimination between two concurrent sound streams (85.4 s) compared to song versus silence (16.9 s) might reflect additional evidence accumulation and temporal integration requirements.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 is explicitly speculative ("might reflect") and proposes a cognitive mechanism for the observed latency difference. While the interpretation is plausible, alternative explanations (e.g., increased task difficulty, different decision criteria, interference between streams) are not excluded. The speculation is reasonable but unsupported by direct evidence.

results.result: Male C57Bl/6 mice produce ultrasonic courtship vocalizations in response to female urine, consisting of frequency-modulated syllables with bimodal duration distribution (23 ms and 88 ms peaks), restricted to 68-84 kHz frequency range with peak at 76 kHz, and organized in temporally regular sequences with inter-syllable intervals around 104 ms.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these basic characterizations of male mouse songs without challenge. All reviewers acknowledged the study's clear description of vocal patterns and acoustic structure, with one noting 'the acoustic structure of the vocal signals was well described' and another praising the 'well-designed' approach.

results.result: Female mice (n=29 sessions, 83 total mice aged 5-11 weeks in fertile cycle stage) significantly discriminate between song playback and silence in a place preference assay (p=0.0088), demonstrating approach response after 16.9 s of playback, with male bedding odor present to increase motivation.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the behavioral effect, Reviewer 1 raised significant concerns about interpretation: 'we cannot determine if it is a general preference for a sound or a specific preference for male songs because only the difference between the presence of song or silence is tested.' Reviewer 3 noted confusion about terminology, stating the measure is 'dwell time' not true 'approach,' making the experimental design incomplete for the stated conclusions.

results.result: Female approach behavior is insensitive to syllable sequence order (randomization: p=0.90) and temporal reversal (p=0.16), indicating females do not rely on global sequential structure but may monitor presence/absence of syllable types independent of order, reinterpreting previous findings about syntactic discrimination.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as solid and novel. The editor noted 'solid evidence' and Reviewer 2 stated 'the confirmation that a lot of other modifications are less determining for the attractiveness of the vocalizations provides solid data on which to base future work.' The insightful manipulations were praised for linking to previous results.

results.result: Female behavior is robust to removal of fast spectro-temporal structure in syllables, showing no preference between intact songs versus phase-scrambled (p=0.79) or pure tone sequences at peak frequency (p=0.97), suggesting sound energy at natural syllable frequency with natural temporal organization is sufficient to drive approach.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 specifically noted these results as novel and valuable, stating they 'provide solid data on which to base future work' and that 'the confirmation that a lot of other modifications are less determining for the attractiveness' is important for the field.

results.result: Females are highly sensitive to disruption of temporal regularity, preferentially approaching intact over irregular songs (p=0.00023), with preference emerging after 85.4 s of playback. Temporal regularity was the only acoustic feature among those tested that females extracted from male courtship displays.
results.evaluation: All reviewers strongly endorsed this as the key finding. The editor called it 'valuable work' with 'solid' evidence. Reviewer 2 stated 'the most interesting outcome of the study is that female mice prefer regularly timed sequences' and noted this 'result is novel and adds to our understanding.' Reviewer 2 predicted 'substantial impact on the field of mouse communication because the regularity of spacing has not been a focus of previous research.'

results.result: Females show no preference between intact and super-regular songs (p=0.15), suggesting natural song rhythmicity is already at ceiling for perceptual saliency and attractiveness, and cannot be improved by additional regularization of syllable onsets.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this finding without objection. It was treated as a logical complement to the temporal regularity result, helping to define the boundaries of the effect. The finding was discussed as part of the overall pattern showing sensitivity to regularity but not to improvements beyond natural levels.

results.result: Female mice monitor temporal regularity in male songs during courtship while showing behavioral invariance to changes in sequential organization or fine acoustic structure of syllables, demonstrating selective extraction of specific acoustic features in ethologically valid behavior.
results.evaluation: Reviewers endorsed this summary conclusion. The editor stated the work 'advances our understanding of the acoustic features driving the attraction of female mice to male vocalisations' with 'solid' evidence. Reviewer 2 noted the study 'will likely have a substantial impact on the field' and provides a clear picture of which features matter.

results.result: Temporal regularity may represent an acoustic signature of singer fitness (linked to breathing patterns and potentially disrupted by irregular breathing or inability to sustain vocal production), serving as an evolutionarily conserved strategy for sensory compression of complex vocal sequences.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about overinterpretation. Reviewer 1 stated the interpretation of 'compressed acoustic features' is 'questionable' and an 'overinterpretation,' arguing the preference may simply reflect deviation from typical parameters rather than compression. Reviewer 2 noted 'the discussion steps beyond the results in a few respects, in particular when trying to determine the underlying reasons for the preference for regularly spaced sequences.'

results.result: The preference for song over silence was robust to different speaker zone lengths, evident in the vast majority of animals, sustained over sessions, and similar across trials. Sessions with side bias (29% ± 7%) were excluded from analysis.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 expressed concern about the side bias exclusion method, stating 'I am a bit worried about their method of removing side bias (29% of trials)' because 'this exclusion of mice exhibiting a side bias is also excluding, specifically, behavior that would be incorrect.' This raises questions about whether the exclusion criteria may have biased results.

results.result: Individual variability in behavioral responses shows roughly one-third of animals with strong preference for intact song, one-third preferring modified songs, and remaining animals as 'swing voters' across different manipulations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raised significant concerns about lack of individual-level analysis: 'There is no analysis of individual preference across tests and we might have the feeling that the effect shown mostly depends on the preference of only a few animals.' The reviewer requested deeper analysis of 'swing voters' and animals consistently choosing modified songs, noting 'there is no discussion of these aspects either.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C15-C17, C33, C66 regarding behavioral invariance to syllable acoustic manipulations. Both evaluations rate these findings as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate statistics and sample sizes; peer reviewers specifically praised these null results as novel and valuable for the field.

Perfect agreement on claims C20-C21, C44, C71-C72 regarding super-regular timing manipulation. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the ceiling effect interpretation while acknowledging alternative explanations; peer reviewers accepted this finding as a logical complement to the temporal regularity result without objection.

Strong agreement on summary claims C22, C27, C53. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the distinction between perceptual sensitivity and behavioral relevance; peer reviewers endorsed the conclusions with the editor calling it 'solid evidence' that 'advances understanding' of acoustic features.

Strong agreement on claims C1-C5 characterizing male mouse vocalizations. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights quantitative measurements and appropriate sample sizes; peer reviewers accepted these characterizations without challenge, praising the 'well-described' acoustic structure.

Strong agreement on claims C18-C19, C67-C69 regarding temporal regularity preference. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes strong statistical evidence and robustness; peer reviewers strongly endorsed this as the key finding with 'substantial impact,' though peer result also includes broader claims C36-C37 about interpretation.

Strong agreement on claims C12-C14, C32, C63-C65 regarding syllable randomization and sequential structure. Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate interpretation of null results; peer reviewers praised these as 'solid and novel' findings. Peer result also includes contextual claims C28-C31 about prior work and reinterpretation.

Significant disagreement on claims C10-C11 regarding basic preference for male songs. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with appropriate statistics; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, raising concerns that the design cannot distinguish general sound preference from specific song preference, and noting confusion about 'dwell time' vs 'approach' terminology.

Overlapping claims C10, C62 but different concerns. OpenEval R2 rates basic preference as SUPPORTED; peer R10 rates as UNCERTAIN due to lack of individual-level analysis, noting 'no analysis of individual preference across tests' and concern that effects may depend on only a few animals.

Overlapping methodological claims C55-C60 about experimental design. OpenEval rates methods as SUPPORTED with adequate documentation; peer reviewers embedded these in R2 rated as UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about the experimental design's ability to test stated conclusions and terminology issues.

Overlapping speculative claims C23, C43, C54 about fitness signaling and functional interpretations. Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes these are explicitly speculative requiring additional evidence; peer reviewers similarly note 'overinterpretation' and that 'discussion steps beyond the results.' Peer R8 also includes production mechanism claims C38-C40.

Overlapping claims C38-C40 regarding vocal production mechanisms. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations and contextualization; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN within broader concerns about overinterpretation of 'compressed acoustic features' and stepping beyond results.

Overlapping claim C73 about side bias exclusion. OpenEval rates methodological details as SUPPORTED with transparent reporting; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, expressing concern that excluding 29% of trials for side bias may specifically exclude incorrect behavior and bias results.

Overlapping claims C61-C62 about temporal dynamics and robustness. OpenEval includes these in SUPPORTED evaluation of basic preference; peer reviewers raise concerns about side bias exclusion methodology in relation to these robustness claims.

Overlapping claims C29, C31 about syllable order and reinterpretation of prior work. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED but notes speculation requiring direct testing; peer reviewers embedded these in broader SUPPORTED evaluation of syllable randomization findings without specific comment on the reinterpretation claims.

Overlapping claims C28, C30 citing prior work on sequential structure. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED for accurately describing prior findings; peer reviewers embedded these contextual claims in their SUPPORTED evaluation of the syllable randomization results.

Overlapping claim C27 about distinguishing perceptual capacity from behavioral relevance. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, emphasizing this distinction with citations on reinforcement learning; peer reviewers included this in their SUPPORTED summary evaluation without specific comment on the perceptual vs. behavioral distinction.

OpenEval evaluated claims C6-C9 about prior work on female preference and male song function as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval evaluated claims C34-C35 about temporal pattern importance in other behavioral contexts as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these comparative context claims.

OpenEval evaluated claims C41-C42 about perceptual benefits of temporal regularity as SUPPORTED with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these mechanistic context claims.

OpenEval evaluated claims C45-C46 about neural coding and cross-modal extrapolation as UNCERTAIN, noting C46 is explicitly speculative without direct auditory evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these neural mechanism claims.

OpenEval evaluated claims C47-C52 about vocal timing across species and neural oscillations as SUPPORTED for citations but noting C49 is more speculative about auditory processing constraints. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these cross-species and theoretical context claims.

OpenEval evaluated claim C70 about cognitive mechanisms for latency differences as UNCERTAIN, noting it is explicitly speculative without excluding alternative explanations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific cognitive interpretation claim.
